input.instructions: Create a compact, accurate blueprint for an 8-to-12-minute educational lesson with exactly ten sequential teaching beats. Do not write full narration. Create exactly three measurable learning objectives. For every beat, provide one distinct complete factual claim, a concrete example, a concise editable visual direction, and one or two exact supplied source IDs. End the claim, example, and visual direction with complete punctuation. Every cited source excerpt must directly support the claim; reuse at least two important technical terms from each cited excerpt so support can be checked locally. Do not invent course assignments, policies, measurements, datasets, instruction encodings, or product behavior that is absent from the supplied excerpts. Keep the claim, example, and visual direction compact; a deterministic local expander will produce the full narration. Sequence the beats from foundations through application and end with a practical analysis checklist. Use only the supplied source excerpts for factual claims. Every factual claim must cite one or more supplied source IDs. Narration must describe information that is essential to understand visuals. Do not imitate a named creator or invent sources.
input.prompt:
Topic: CSCI-538: Puzzles for Computing. Create a representative course-foundations companion aligned to the official catalog description. It must teach durable concepts and problem-solving methods without claiming to replace the instructor's syllabus. Official catalog description: In this course, students will explore puzzle solving and creation as a way of exploring human-inspired algorithm development and the synergy of humans and computers to develop programmatic solutions. Many different types of puzzles will be explored, including logical puzzles, mazes, optimization puzzles, and word puzzles. For each type of puzzle, students will develop and implement both optimal solving algorithms and algorithms that mimic human solving processes. They will also write programs that construct certain types of puzzles with human solvers in mind. Finally, they will discuss and solve puzzle hunts, which include puzzles without any instruction and apparent ambiguity, yet are still uniquely solvable for humans. Prerequisites: CSCI-261 or CSCI-264 or IGME-309 or equivalent course. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Spring Regeneration revision 1: use ten distinct, specific beat titles and avoid repeating any title or section label.

Source excerpts:

[mit-algorithms]
Algorithm analysis connects a precise problem specification to a correctness argument and resource bounds. Asymptotic notation describes how resource use grows with input size. A loop invariant supports a proof by initialization, maintenance, and termination. Divide-and-conquer algorithms split a problem, solve subproblems, and combine their results. Recurrences describe the cost of recursive algorithms. Graph algorithms operate on vertices and edges to answer reachability, ordering, connectivity, and path questions. Dynamic programming records solutions to overlapping subproblems. Core methods include sorting, hashing, trees, graphs, shortest paths, and dynamic programming. A disciplined solution states inputs and outputs, proves correctness, and then analyzes time and space.

[opendsa]
OpenDSA presents data structures and algorithms through executable visualizations and exercises. Lists represent ordered sequences with position-based operations. Stacks use last-in, first-out access, while queues use first-in, first-out access. Trees represent hierarchical relationships and support recursive traversals. Hash tables map keys to locations and require a collision strategy. Graphs can be represented with adjacency structures for traversal and path algorithms. Automata and formal languages describe machines, accepted strings, and computational limits. Representation choices and invariants determine which operations are efficient and which errors are possible.

[rit-csci-538]
In this course, students will explore puzzle solving and creation as a way of exploring human-inspired algorithm development and the synergy of humans and computers to develop programmatic solutions. Many different types of puzzles will be explored, including logical puzzles, mazes, optimization puzzles, and word puzzles. For each type of puzzle, students will develop and implement both optimal solving algorithms and algorithms that mimic human solving processes. They will also write programs that construct certain types of puzzles with human solvers in mind. Finally, they will discuss and solve puzzle hunts, which include puzzles without any instruction and apparent ambiguity, yet are still uniquely solvable for humans. Prerequisites: CSCI-261 or CSCI-264 or IGME-309 or equivalent course. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Spring

beats.claim: CSCI-538 explores puzzle solving and creation to examine human-inspired algorithm development and human-computer synergy in programmatic solutions.
beats.example: Students will analyze how a maze-solving program can be designed to mimic human backtracking rather than using a purely optimal breadth-first search.
beats.title: Course Foundations and Scope
beats.visualDirection: Display a split-screen graphic: left side shows a grid maze with a red optimal path, right side shows the same maze with a winding human-like path that occasionally backtracks.

beats.claim: Logical puzzles require constraint satisfaction techniques where each clue restricts possible values until a unique solution emerges.
beats.example: A Sudoku solver uses backtracking to assign digits 1-9 to empty cells while maintaining row, column, and box constraints.
beats.title: Logical Puzzles and Constraint Satisfaction
beats.visualDirection: Show a 9x9 grid with highlighted constraints (e.g., a red circle around a row) and a step-by-step animation of a cell being filled based on eliminated options.

beats.claim: Maze solving relies on graph algorithms that treat intersections as vertices and corridors as edges to find paths efficiently.
beats.example: A depth-first search explores one corridor until a dead end, then backtracks to try an alternative route, mirroring human exploration.
beats.title: Maze Algorithms and Graph Traversal
beats.visualDirection: Render a graph maze with nodes and edges, highlighting the DFS traversal path in blue and the backtracking steps in gray.

beats.claim: Optimization puzzles seek the best possible solution under constraints, often using heuristics to approximate optimal results when exact methods are too slow.
beats.example: A traveling salesman puzzle uses nearest-neighbor heuristics to quickly generate a route, even if it is not mathematically optimal.
beats.title: Optimization Puzzles and Heuristics
beats.visualDirection: Display a city map with cities as nodes and roads as edges, showing a heuristic path in green versus a shorter optimal path in red.

beats.claim: Word puzzles utilize string manipulation and dictionary lookups to match patterns, anagrams, or cross-references efficiently.
beats.example: A crossword solver checks candidate words against a dictionary using prefix matching to validate partial fills.
beats.title: Word Puzzles and String Processing
beats.visualDirection: Show a crossword grid with a candidate word list scrolling on the side, highlighting matches that fit the existing letter pattern.

beats.claim: Each puzzle type maps to specific data structures and algorithms, such as stacks for backtracking, hash tables for dictionary lookups, and graphs for pathfinding.
beats.example: A stack stores the sequence of moves in a maze solver, allowing the program to reverse steps when a dead end is reached.
beats.title: Algorithmic Paradigms and Data Structures
beats.visualDirection: Illustrate a stack data structure with maze move coordinates being pushed and popped, synchronized with the maze grid animation.

beats.claim: Programmers can implement algorithms that mimic human cognitive strategies, such as pattern recognition and trial-and-error, alongside mathematically optimal methods.
beats.example: A word puzzle solver might prioritize common letters first, just as humans do, rather than exhaustively checking every permutation.
beats.title: Human-Inspired vs. Optimal Approaches
beats.visualDirection: Show a side-by-side comparison: left side displays a decision tree for optimal search, right side shows a branching path that prioritizes high-frequency letters.

beats.claim: Creating puzzles requires designing constraints that guarantee a unique solution while remaining solvable for humans without external hints.
beats.example: A puzzle generator validates each clue against a solution set to ensure no contradictions exist and that the puzzle is uniquely solvable.
beats.title: Puzzle Generation and Human Solvability
beats.visualDirection: Display a puzzle generation pipeline: input constraints -> solver verification -> ambiguity check -> final puzzle output.

beats.claim: Puzzle hunts present instruction-free challenges with apparent ambiguity, yet they remain uniquely solvable through logical deduction and contextual reasoning.
beats.example: A hunt puzzle might use a series of interconnected clues where each answer reveals the next, requiring solvers to infer connections without explicit rules.
beats.title: Puzzle Hunts and Ambiguity Resolution
beats.visualDirection: Show a puzzle hunt board with interconnected clue cards, highlighting how solving one card unlocks the next through inferred relationships.

beats.claim: Students must verify puzzle design by checking for unique solvability, constraint consistency, and appropriate difficulty scaling before deployment.
beats.example: A checklist confirms that every clue is necessary, no alternative solutions exist, and the puzzle aligns with the target algorithmic paradigm.
beats.title: Practical Analysis Checklist
beats.visualDirection: Display a checklist graphic with three boxes: 'Unique Solution Verified', 'Constraint Consistency Checked', 'Difficulty Aligned', each with a toggle switch for pass/fail.

learningObjectives: Define the four primary puzzle categories (logical, maze, optimization, word) and map each to a corresponding algorithmic paradigm.
Explain how human-inspired solving strategies differ from optimal algorithmic approaches and identify when each is appropriate.
Evaluate puzzle hunt design principles by analyzing ambiguity resolution, unique solvability, and instruction-free constraints.
